title_original: Deadline’s Reviews Of This Week’s Box Office Openers: ‘The Only Living Pickpocket In New York’, ‘Gentle Monster,’ ‘Queen At Sea’ & More

blocks.text: This week’s theatrical releases continue the march into movie awards season, with the emergence on U.S. screens of films that started their journeys with buzzy festival launches as far back as Sundance.
Deadline has compiled its list of movies we’ve reviewed across the year that are now hitting cinemas.

This week, that includes Sony Pictures Classics’ The Only Living Pickpocket in New York , which bowed at Sundance and just this week earned star John Turturro a Gotham Award nomination . Also, the Berlin Film Festival award winner Queen at Sea , a family drama featuring the powerful 1-2 punch of Juliette Binoche and Tom Courtenay.

RELATED: 53 Of The Most Anticipated Movies Of 2026 A pair of Netflix movies are also hitting screens before their streaming dates: Léa Seydoux in the Cannes pic Gentle Monster, and Peter Berg’s WWII pic The Mosquito Bowl which just world premiered at AFI Fest.

‘The Only Living Pickpocket In New York’ Image Credit: MRC Release: Wide (October 30) Distributor: Sony Pictures Classics Director-screenwriter: Noah Segan Cast: John Turturro, Steve Buscemi, Giancarlo Esposito, Will Price, Tatiana Maslany Original review date: January 27 (Sundance Film Festival) Deadline’s takeaway: John Turturro’s Harry is a throwback, and so is this movie, a modest but really rather mesmerizing and forlorn film, one that’s curated just as much as it is directed. It’s about things past, about things gone, but also things that won’t stay dead as much as society wants that to happen. It’s also a film about vanishing bohemia, and it’s no coincidence many of the film’s storied leads are played by leading lights of New York’s iconic indie movie scene. — DW RELATED: ‘The Only Living Pickpocket In New York’ Review: John Turturro Steals The Show In Noah Segan’s Mesmerizing Debut – Sundance Film Festival

blocks.text: ‘Gentle Monster’ Image Credit: Frédéric Batier/Netflix Release: Limited (October 30) Distributor: Netflix Director-screenwriter: Marie Kreutzer Cast: Léa Seydoux, Laurence Rupp, Jella Haase, Catherine Deneuve Original review date: May 15 (Cannes Film Festival) Deadline’s takeaway: Léa Seydoux gives a very committed, unaffected performance as an experimental pianist who must deal with the dawning knowledge that her beloved husband has a second life online as a pedophile pornographer in Marie Kreutzer’s measured fictional account of a family torn apart by similar accusations. — SB RELATED: ‘Gentle Monster’ Review: Léa Seydoux Gives A Committed Performance In Cluttered Story Of A Family Torn Apart – Cannes Film Festival

blocks.text: ‘The Mosquito Bowl’ Image Credit: Netflix Release: Limited (October 30) Distributor: Netflix Director: Peter Berg Screenwriters: Peter Berg and Mark L. Smith Cast: Nicholas Galitzine, Bill Skarsgård, Ray Nicholson, Tom Francis, Brent Comer, Jack Ingram, Ella Newton, Peter Berg, Dominic Bogart, Lola Bond, Stacy Clausen, Billy Smith, Steven Sammut, Blake Erickson, Claudia Ware, Pat McAfee Original review date: October 23 (AFI Fest) Deadline’s takeaway: The Mosquito Bowl achieves its true strength by putting us directly into the center of the hell of war, a visceral experience so intense and unrelenting it seems we are there and, like those who were on the front lines, a feeling there is no way out. Fair warning: Peter Berg, whose films have included Lone Survivor, Deep Water Horizon and other tales of valor and courage against all odds, does not hold back in showing war’s true horrors. — PH RELATED: ‘The Mosquito Bowl’ Review: Peter Berg’s Powerful True WWII Story Takes Four Star Players From The Glory Of The Football Field To The Hell Of The Battlefield – AFI Fest

blocks.text: ‘Queen At Sea’ Image Credit: Seafaring LLC Release: Limited (October 30) Distributor: Greenwich Entertainment Director-screenwriter: Lance Hammer Cast: Juliette Binoche, Tom Courtenay, Anna Calder-Marshall, Florence Hunt Original review date: February 19 (Berlin Film Festival) Deadline’s takeaway: The complications this particular family unit is facing are laid out starkly and without any further ado in Queen at Sea ‘s shocking opening moments. It’s a staggeringly bold gambit, but the two grounded, laser-focused leads — Juliette Binoche and Tom Courtenay — help navigate us through the intimate and surprisingly complex moral maze that unfolds. — DW RELATED: ‘Queen At Sea’ Review: Juliette Binoche And Tom Courtenay Light Up A Dark, Intimate Study Of Dementia – Berlin Film Festival

‘Ali G: Who Iz I?’ Image Credit: Amazon MGM Studios / Everett Collection Release: Wide (October 23) Distributor: Amazon MGM Studios Director: Sacha Baron Cohen Screenwriters: Sacha Baron Cohen & Anthony Hines & Peter Baynham & Dan Swimer & Dan Mazer & Keisha Zollar Cast: Sacha Baron Cohen, Morgana Robinson, Marion Robinson, Alphja Miknas, Clive Russell, Stewart Rodeheaver Review date: October 22 Deadline’s takeaway: Sacha Baron Cohen obviously believes the moment is right to bring back his LOL OG as the world has only sunk further into the abyss since his last appearance. While the new film drifts from bit to bit, some straining for laughs, enough of it works to make this feel like vintage Baron Cohen daredevil comedy at the expense of the clueless. — PH RELATED: ‘Ali G: Who Iz I?’ Review: Sacha Baron Cohen’s Signature Prankster Returns In Outrageous Form With Something To Offend Everyone

blocks.text: ‘Clayface’ Image Credit: Warner Bros./Courtesy Everett Collection Release: Wide (October 23) Distributor: Warner Bros/DC Studios Director: James Watkins Screenwriters: Mike Flanagan & Hossein Amini Cast: Tom Rhys Harries, Naomi Ackie, David Dencik, Max Minghella, Eddie Marsan Original review date: October 21 Deadline’s takeaway: Whether you’re a comic book nerd or a horror junkie, Clayface is worth the price of admission for its genre-driven approach to a lesser-known character, hopefully serving as a roadmap for the DCU’s onscreen future. Just maybe brace yourself if you’re squeamish. — GG RELATED: ‘Clayface’ Review: DCU Molds Batman Villain’s Origin Story Into Fun, Scary Body Horror

blocks.text: ‘Klara And The Sun’ Image Credit: Sony / 3000 Pictures Release: Wide (October 23) Distributor: Sony Pictures Director: Taika Waititi Screenwriters: Taika Waititi and Dahvi Waller (based on the book by Kazuo Ishiguro) Cast: Jenna Ortega, Amy Adams, Mia Tharia, Natasha Lyonne, Aran Murphy, Steve Buscemi, Rachel House, Jesse Griffin Original review date: October 15 (London Film Festival) Deadline’s takeaway: Taiki Waititi should be a snug-as-a-bug fit for Kazuo Ishiguro’s dystopian — or is it? — 2021 novel, given the director’s affinity for a very particular and peculiar kind of reality-based cringe comedy. But Klara just doesn’t deliver on any of the fronts it promises. — DW RELATED: ‘Klara And The Sun’ Review: Taika Waititi’s Latest Is A Curiously Flat Dystopian Comedy-Drama – London Film Festival

Grant, Marli Siu, Nabhaan Rizwan, Gustav Lindh, Ella Bruccoleri, Ben Ashenden, Kiell Smith Binoe Original review date: October 22 Deadline’s takeaway: A hit at Sundance where it was picked up by Black Bear , this wry film from writer-directors Alex Huston and Eleanor Wilson is sexy and satirically funny, but also oddly haunting as a truly twisted fable that says its never too late to become your own best version of Cinderella. — PH RELATED: ‘Wicker’ Review: Olivia Colman And Peter Dinklage Turn Alexander Skarsgård Into A Sexy Basket Case In Comic Fable That’s Pure Delight

blocks.text: ‘Wildwood’ Image Credit: Courtesy of Laika Release: Wide (October 23) Distributor: Fathom Director: Travis Knight Screenwriter: Chris Butler (based on the book by Colin Meloy) Cast: Carey Mulligan, Peyton Elizabeth Lee, Jacob Tremblay , Angela Bassett, Mahershala Ali, Awkwafina, Maya Erskine, Jake Johnson, Charlie Day, Tom Waits, Richard E. Grant, Amanda Stenberg, Tantoo Cardinal, Len Cariou, Marc Evan Jackson Original review date: October 11 (London Film Festival) Deadline’s takeaway: The painstaking stop-motion animation process applied to a tale on a scale rarely seen on this level is a visual knockout, and the story is a compelling one focused on a scrappy young heroine determined to fight back and save her baby brother after he is harrowingly abducted from the streets of Portland by a murder of crows. — PH RELATED: ‘Wildwood’ Review: Carey Mulligan Leads Voice Cast Of Laika’s Ambitious And Visually Stunning Stop-Motion Fantasy Epic – London Film Festival

blocks.text: ‘A Talent For Murder’ Image Credit: Bleecker Street/LD Entertainment Release: Wide (October 23) Distributor: Bleecker Street Director: Anton Corbijn Writer: Joanna Murray-Smith Cast: Helen Mirren, Alden Ehrenreich, Olivia Cooke, Juliet Stevenson, James Faulkner Original review date: September 15 (Toronto Film Festival) Deadline’s takeaway: Helen Mirren, playing wildly against type, is a revelation in this flawed but very entertaining two-hander, which belongs in the unique subgenre of literary biographies in which a cult author’s life is investigated through the highly specific prism of their work. — DW RELATED: ‘A Talent For Murder’ Review: Helen Mirren Is Mesmerizing As Tortured Genius Crime Writer Patricia Highsmith – Toronto Film Festival

blocks.text: ‘You Can See Everything’ Image Credit: A24 / Everett Collection Release: Wide (October 23) Distributor: A24 Directors: Nathan Fielder, Lance Oppenheim Cast: Nathan Fielder, Elizabeth Holmes, Billy Evans, Christopher Abbott Original review date: September 7 (Telluride Film Festival) Deadline’s takeaway: The unusual (to say the least) documentary, which was shot in secrecy and runs nearly 3 hours, is unlike any I have ever seen in terms of pure access. blocks.text: ‘Love Language’ Image Credit: SXSW Release: Limited (October 23) Distributor: Vertical Director-screenwriter: Joey Power Cast: Chloë Grace Moretz, Anthony Ramos, Manny Jacinto, Isabel May, Lukas Gage, Billie Lourd, Chloe Fineman, Zach Zucker, Morgan Jay, Bobbi Althoff, Marchánt Davis, Dan Perrault Original review date: March 17 (SXSW) Deadline’s takeaway: Love Language is a return to classic rom-com form, with heart and humor, as well as a talented ensemble cast that beautifully brings Joey Power’s script to life against a dreamy Chicago backdrop. — GG RELATED: ‘Love Language’ Review: Chloë Grace Moretz Leads Messy Love Triangle While Capitalizing On Untapped Wedding Vows Market — SXSW

blocks.text: ‘Possible Love’ Image Credit: Joo Jae-bum/Netflix Release: Limited (October 23) Distributor: Netflix Director: Lee Chang-dong Screenwriters: Lee Chang-dong and Oh Jung-Mi Cast: Jeon Do-Yeon, Sul Kyung-gu, Zo In-sung, Cho Yeo-Jeung Original review date: September 6 (Venice Film Festival) Deadline’s takeaway: In some ways Lee Chang-dong‘s first film in eight years, which is South Korea’s official entry into the International Feature Film Oscar race , might remind you of the class divide in Bong Joon Ho’s Oscar-winning Parasite . But with a pandemic between that release and this one, Lee’s film carries a poignant subtext: a certain desire for love and longing in a world more split apart than ever, and one which for many seems like it all is out of reach. — PH RELATED: ‘Possible Love’ Review: Lee Chang -dong’s South Korean International Oscar Entry Is Powerful Story Of Class And Desire – Venice Film Festival
